area: Area VI. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how true airspeed and bank angle set the rate of turn, estimate the standard-rate bank with the IFH rules of thumb, teach the entry and recovery of standard-rate and half-standard-rate turns on round dials and on glass, full panel and partial panel, coach coordination and trim in the turn, fly a turn to instrument standards while explaining it, and analyze and correct the common turn errors an examiner simulates.
why: In a prolonged constant-rate turn the inner ear stops sensing the turn, the roll-out feels like a turn the other way, and a pilot who rolls back in can lose control [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. Overbanking without adjusting pitch can end in a diving spiral, where more back pressure only tightens the turn [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. Standard rate is the main reference for bank angle [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] and leaves the pilot time to cross-check [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. The CFII PTS wants it taught full panel and partial panel because of fatal spatial disorientation accidents of instrument-rated pilots maneuvering in cloud with failed gyros or a lost electronic display [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]].

chunks.title: What the examiner looks for in Task B

body.p: **Teaching turns** is Task B of Area VI. You describe the relationship of true airspeed and angle of bank to a standard-rate turn, the entry and recovery of a constant-rate turn full panel and partial panel including a half-standard-rate turn, and coordination and trim; then the common errors; then you demonstrate while explaining, and analyze and correct simulated errors [[FAA-S-8081-9E:32|PTS VI.B]]. The Area NOTE has the evaluator select Task H and at least one other Task, and you teach with the method you chose, primary and supporting or control and performance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:32|PTS Area VI NOTE]].

The general material is in the straight-and-level lesson FII.VI.A: the two methods, what the PTS words mean and how they are graded, the exchange of flight controls, and how to simulate failures safely. This lesson builds on it and stays on what a turn adds. The Instrument lesson IR.IV.A covers the pilot's side of turns, and the CFI lesson AI.XI.D covers turns to headings and compass turns for VFR learners.

body.p: Why standard rate: a turn of 3° per second gives a timely heading change and still leaves time to cross-check and avoid drastic changes in the forces on the airplane. At no time should the airplane be maneuvered faster than the pilot can comfortably cross-check, and most autopilots turn at standard rate [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

callout.text: Application: give the student the one-line idea before any numbers. "A turn is straight-and-level with a bank in it. Everything you know still works; the turn adds a bank to set, lost lift to replace and a heading to lead."

check.q: The examiner picks Task B and asks you to teach a partial panel turn. You chose control and performance. Should you still know which instrument is primary for bank in each phase?
check.a: Yes. The evaluator determines that you demonstrate and fully understand your chosen method [[FAA-S-8081-9E:17|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]], both methods use the same instruments and control responses [[23:135|IFH 6-2]], and the IFH describes turns in primary and supporting terms [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

chunks.title: True airspeed, bank and rate of turn

body.p: **The relationship of true airspeed and angle of bank to a standard rate turn.** Rate of turn comes from bank and speed together. Same bank, faster: the rate drops and the radius grows. Same speed, more bank: the rate rises and the radius shrinks [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. The IFH calls standard rate the main reference for bank angle, so a pilot must know how the bank changes with speed, for example when slowing for holding or an approach [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

The PHAK gives the formula behind the picture: rate of turn in degrees per second equals 1,091 times the tangent of the bank, divided by the airspeed in knots, and all airspeed in that section is true airspeed [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. So the bank for 3° per second depends on TAS, not on the indicated airspeed. The IFH puts it in plain words: the bank needed for a given rate of turn is proportional to the true airspeed [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

bullets: Normal standard-rate banks run 10° to 20° [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].
In Figure 4-15, 30° of bank gives 6.5° per second at 100 knots but only 3.2° per second at 200 knots [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].
At 400 mph a standard-rate turn takes about 44° of bank, and then only about 79 percent of the lift is vertical [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].
Speed also sets the radius: at a higher speed a course intercept needs more distance and a longer lead [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].
Holding without RNAV guidance: turns at 3° per second, 30° of bank, or 25° with a flight director, whichever needs the least bank [[33:391|AIM 5-3-8]].

callout.text: Application: teach it as two inputs and one result. Bank and true airspeed go in, rate of turn comes out. Ask, "You slow from 120 to 90 knots in the hold and keep the same bank. What happens to the rate?" Figure 4-15 gives the answer: it goes up [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

check.q: Your student asks why a jet needs a steeper bank than her trainer for the same standard-rate turn. What do you say?
check.a: Rate of turn depends on bank and true airspeed. At a higher TAS the same bank gives a lower rate, so the bank must increase to keep 3° per second [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

chunks.title: The bank-angle rules of thumb, and where the IFH gives two

body.p: The IFH turns chapter gives a rule of thumb for the standard-rate bank: 15 percent of the true airspeed. Divide the airspeed by 10 and add half the result: 100 knots needs about 15°, 120 knots about 18° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. The glass chapter repeats the same rule and examples [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

The aerodynamics chapter gives a different one: divide the airspeed by ten and add 7, so 90 knots takes 16° [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. Application: the two rules agree near 140 knots and drift apart on either side. The table compares them with the PHAK formula [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]] solved for 3° per second.

body.p: Either rule is only a start. Set the approximate bank on the attitude indicator, then check the turn coordinator or turn rate indicator and adjust the bank for standard rate [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. Application: teach the 15 percent rule as the main one, since the IFH uses it for instrument turns on both panels, and mention the other so the student is not thrown when she meets it.

Use the true airspeed. The rule says true airspeed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] and the PHAK formula uses TAS [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. On the PFD in Figure 7-67 (in the glass section below) the tape shows 120 knots and the TAS box 126 knots [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]. Application: 126 knots gives about 19°, a degree more than the indicated speed suggests.

**Small heading changes** use less than standard rate. The IFH gives three versions: bank about equal to the degrees to turn, not over 30° [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]; no more than the degrees to turn and never more than a standard-rate bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; and, better defined, half the heading change but never more than standard rate [[23:213|IFH 7-52]].

callout.text: Standard-rate bank: TAS ÷ 10, plus half. Lead: half the bank. Small change: half the degrees to turn, never past standard rate.

check.q: Flying 90 knots, your student uses "airspeed over ten plus seven," sets 16° and the turn coordinator shows more than standard rate. Is her rule wrong?
check.a: It is an IFH rule [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], but at 90 knots it gives more bank than the 15 percent rule's 13.5° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Any rule is a start: she adjusts the bank until the turn coordinator shows standard rate [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

chunks.title: Full panel on round dials: entering the turn

body.p: **Technique and procedure using full panel for entry** of a constant-rate turn on analog instruments:

bullets: Roll in with coordinated aileron and rudder in the direction of the turn. Pilots commonly roll in much too fast; in early training, base the control pressures on the rate of cross-check and interpretation [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

Set the approximate bank on the attitude indicator, then check the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft for standard rate, and note the exact bank on the banking scale when it shows standard rate [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
Once the turn is established, the turn coordinator is primary for bank and the attitude indicator supports [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

During the roll-in, check the altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator: vertical lift drops as the bank increases, so pitch must come up [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. IFH 4-11 suggests half-bar-width steps [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].
To hold airspeed, the airspeed indicator is primary for power, and the throttle comes up as drag increases [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
As the bank is established, trim off the pressures from the pitch and power changes [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

body.p: Figure 7-33 also labels the heading indicator "Primary bank". Read it with the text: in the established turn the turn coordinator is primary, and the heading indicator becomes primary for bank only when the wings are approximately level after the roll-out [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

body.p: In control-and-performance words the same entry reads: set the bank and the slightly higher pitch on the attitude indicator and the extra power on the power instruments, trim, cross-check the turn coordinator, altimeter and airspeed, and adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

callout.text: Application: on the first turn lesson, have the student roll in slowly enough to name each instrument as she checks it: "bank 15, turn coordinator on the mark, altimeter steady, airspeed steady, trim." If she cannot keep up with her own words, the roll is faster than her cross-check [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

check.q: Your student rolls into a standard-rate turn in two seconds, then chases altitude for the next 20. What do you tell her?
check.a: Pilots commonly roll in much too fast; base the roll rate on how fast she can cross-check and interpret, because maneuvering faster than that only creates corrections [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Check pitch as soon as bank pressure starts [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

chunks.title: Full panel on round dials: leading and rolling out

body.p: **Recovery of a constant rate turn.** As long as the airplane is in a coordinated bank it keeps turning, so the roll-out starts before the heading. Lead by half the bank: with 10° of bank, start 5° early. The lead really depends on rate of turn, bank and rate of recovery, so practice with half the bank until the student knows the lead her own technique needs [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

bullets: Roll out with coordinated aileron and rudder opposite the turn, at the same rate used to roll in; that makes the lead predictable, especially partial panel [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
When the roll-out starts, the attitude indicator becomes primary for bank; once the wings are about level, the heading indicator is primary, as in straight-and-level [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
Vertical lift returns as the bank comes off: lower the pitch, and adjust power and trim as lift and airspeed change [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].
After the roll-out, keep the straight-and-level cross-check going; dropping it commonly follows a perfectly executed turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].
Check for precession: if the heading keeps changing with the attitude indicator showing level flight and the ball centered, the attitude gyro has precessed [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

body.p: Some airplanes are very stable in turns and need only slight trim; others need constant, rapid cross-check to stop an overbanking tendency. Because pitch, bank and airspeed errors feed each other in a turn, the cross-check must be fast to prevent an accumulation of errors [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

Turn the shortest way unless there is a reason not to. The IFH shortcut for a reciprocal: over 180, subtract 200 and add 20; under 180, add 200 and subtract 20. From 305° the reciprocal is 125°, so a turn to 110° goes right [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

callout.text: Application: treat the lead as a skill to calibrate, not a number to memorize. Have the student call her roll-out point aloud, then grade the result: "3° past, so start 3° earlier next time." With consistent roll-in and roll-out rates the right lead can be found [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

check.q: Your student rolls out of every turn on heading but about 80 feet high. What is she missing?
check.a: She does not lower the pitch as the vertical lift component increases during the roll-out, which gives a consistent altitude gain on recovery [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Bring the pitch down as the bank comes off, then retrim [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

chunks.title: Full panel on glass: the turn rate indicator

body.p: On a PFD the turn uses finer tools. Estimate the bank, set it on the attitude indicator, then cross-check the turn rate indicator on the HSI and adjust the bank slightly. The turn rate indicator is primary for bank because it is the only instrument that can show a standard-rate turn exactly; the attitude indicator sets the bank, as a control instrument, and supports by showing whether the bank is more or less than calculated [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

bullets: The roll scale is marked at 0°, 10°, 20°, 30°, 45° and 60° [[23:153|IFH 6-20]], and the roll pointer shows bank to about 1° [[23:199|IFH 7-38]].

On the IFH example display the turn rate trend vector shows the heading 6 seconds ahead. The second tick mark is standard rate; past it the turn is faster than standard [[23:159|IFH 6-26]] [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].
Roll-in: as vertical lift drops, add aft pressure enough to stop any altitude loss trend, add power for the extra drag, then trim off the forces [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

Roll-out: the same rate as the roll-in. The attitude indicator is primary for bank during the transition and the heading indicator once the wings are level; lower the pitch with the bank so it reaches level pitch at zero bank [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].
The turn rate indicator sits on the compass rose, which helps judge when to start the roll-out [[23:213|IFH 7-52]].

body.p: The IFH lead example: from 030° to 120° with a 15° standard-rate bank, lead by 7.5° and start the roll-out at about 112°. How much the turn over- or undershoots tells the pilot how to adjust the lead [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

callout.text: Glass invites fixation. Students tend to give all their attention to the turn rate indicator and drop the rest of the cross-check; a modified radial scan works well in the turn [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]. New pilots also fixate on trend vectors in general [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

check.q: Your glass student holds 18° on the roll scale because the rule of thumb said so, but the trend vector sits past the second tick mark. What do you say?
check.a: The turn rate indicator, not the bank number, is primary for bank: shallow the bank until the vector sits on the second tick mark [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]. The exact bank for standard rate varies with true airspeed [[23:213|IFH 7-52]].

body.p: **Including the performance of a half-standard rate turn.** At standard rate the airplane turns 45° in 15 seconds; at half standard rate it takes 30 seconds. The IFH uses half standard rate for small heading changes in timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

body.p: Where your student will meet it in IFR flying:

bullets: Small heading changes in timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
No-gyro radar approach: all turns at standard rate, and after the controller turns the airplane onto final, turns at half standard rate [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]] [[23:309|IFH 10-18]].
The IFH example of a localizer intercept from a DME arc: the lead radial gives 7° of lead, so a half-standard-rate turn is used until the localizer needle starts to move [[23:262|IFH 9-19]].

callout.text: Application: teach half standard rate as its own picture, not as a sloppy standard-rate turn. Calibrate it once with the clock, have the student note where the miniature aircraft or the trend vector sits, and use that picture for every small heading change and for the no-gyro final.

check.q: On a practice no-gyro approach the controller says turns are now half standard rate. How long should a 15° turn take?
check.a: Ten seconds. Half standard rate turns 45° in 30 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], so 15° takes 10; no-gyro turns after the turn onto final are made at half standard rate [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]].

Ball, every time the turn coordinator is read: once the roll stops it shows only direction and rate of turn, so do not assume the turn comes from a bank unless the ball is centered [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]

body.p: The timed turn: the clock replaces the heading indicator. Start the roll-in as the second hand passes a cardinal point, hold the calibrated standard rate (or half standard rate for small changes), and roll out when the computed seconds are up. If roll-in and roll-out rates match, the entry and recovery time need not be counted [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. That is why the IFH stresses matching them, especially partial panel [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

Calibrate the turn coordinator first: hold the standard-rate indication and note the heading every 10 seconds; a true standard-rate turn changes 30°. If it turns more or less, use a smaller or larger deflection. Do it in each direction and use the corrected deflections in all timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Practice timed turns full panel first and check them on the heading indicator; without it, check on the compass after the turn, allowing for deviation [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Turns to compass headings are Task F.

callout.text: Application: before you cover the gyros, fly one calibration turn each way with the student calling the heading every 10 seconds. The "doghouse" [[23:116|IFH 5-21]] then becomes a number she has checked herself, and it is the same picture she will fly with the gyros covered.

check.q: Partial panel, your student must turn from 090° to 180° at standard rate. How long, and what does she use for bank?
check.a: 90° at 3° per second is 30 seconds, rolling in as the second hand passes a cardinal point [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Bank comes from the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft, with the ball centered [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

chunks.title: Partial panel on glass: an AHRS failure in the turn

body.p: **Partial panel** on an electronic display means the AHRS is simulated or rendered inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. In the IFH example an AHRS failure removes all attitude and heading indications from the PFD and all unusual attitude protection; the autopilot keeps only roll and altitude hold [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

bullets: The slip/skid indicator is gone too, and that airplane has no standby turn coordinator. The magnetic compass is left, and it is not as useful as a turn coordinator or slip/skid indicator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

The standby instruments are an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass. The analog attitude indicator can tumble in extreme pitch and at high bank angles [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Application: keep partial panel turns at or below standard rate.
After an AHRS or magnetometer failure, timed turns are used instead of compass turns because they are simpler: they need no allowance for compass errors [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

In the IFH example the autopilot's roll mode, a wing leveler, takes its information from a turn coordinator behind the MFD that the pilot cannot see; with an AHRS and ADC failure the manufacturer recommends using it to cut workload [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

body.p: Calibrate on glass with the PFD working: start the timer as the compass card passes a cardinal heading and stop it at the next; 90° should take 30 seconds. If not, fly a deflection above or below the standard-rate mark, and calibrate both directions [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

The IFH does not say which bank reference to use for a timed turn once the AHRS failure has taken the turn rate indicator too. Application: in an airplane like the IFH example, that leaves the standby attitude indicator for the bank, set to the rule-of-thumb bank, with the clock for the heading change and the compass checked after the roll-out. Teach from the AFM supplement of the airplane you fly.

check.q: With the AHRS simulated failed, your glass student asks how to make a 60° heading change. What do you teach?
check.a: A timed turn, which is simpler than a compass turn [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]: 20 seconds at standard rate [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], the bank set on the standby attitude indicator (Application), and the compass read after the roll-out in steady flight [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. In the IFH example no slip/skid indicator or standby turn coordinator is left [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

chunks.title: Coordination of controls and trim in the turn

body.p: **Coordination of controls and trim.** Any aileron input produces adverse yaw: in a right roll the left wing's extra lift brings extra induced drag, which yaws the nose left at first. Rudder on entry and exit corrects it, and it is needed for precise control on instruments [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

body.p: Power is part of coordination. The higher angle of attack that holds altitude in the bank adds induced drag, so airspeed drops unless power is added, and the thrust needed grows with the bank [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]] [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]. Added power also makes the airplane yaw and roll left unless aileron and rudder counter it [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

Trim: as the bank is established, trim off the pressures from the pitch and power changes [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. If trim is used to hold the turn, it has to be removed once the turn is complete [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. Check the ball throughout the turn, especially if pressures are held instead of trimmed off [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Unless the airplane is trimmed, it is hard to tell whether a pressure change comes from the aerodynamics or from her own hands [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

callout.text: Application: show what trim buys in a turn. Trim the established turn, relax your grip, and let the student watch whether the bank holds. Some airplanes hold it with only slight trim and some overbank and need constant cross-check [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; she should know which kind she flies.

check.q: In a right standard-rate turn the ball sits right of center. What is happening and what is the fix?
check.a: The ball is off center toward the turn, so the airplane is slipping: banked too much for its rate of turn. Add right rudder or reduce the bank [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

chunks.title: Risk: overbanking, the spiral and the inner ear

body.p: The inner ear senses a turn as it starts, but the fluid in the canal takes about 15 to 20 seconds to catch up. In a constant-rate turn the pilot then feels no turn, and the roll-out feels like a turn the other way, so she may roll back into the original turn [[23:71|IFH 3-4]] [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. The airplane tends to lose altitude in a turn; feeling level, the pilot pulls back and tightens the turn, the graveyard spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. A head movement in a long turn can set off the Coriolis illusion, so dropped items are picked up with minimal head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

**Overbanking.** Overbanking without adjusting pitch takes more and more elevator pressure, until more back pressure only tightens the turn without raising the nose [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. A rapid downward movement of the altimeter or VSI needle, with rising airspeed, despite back pressure, is a diving spiral. Recovery [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]:

bullets: Shallow the bank at once with smooth, coordinated aileron and rudder, holding or slightly relaxing elevator pressure [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].
Speed up the cross-check of attitude indicator, altimeter and VSI, and reduce power if the airspeed increase is rapid [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].
When the elevator is effective again, hold the bank shown and set the nose-high attitude that bank needs [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

body.p: Setting it up safely: the general rules are in FII.VI.A (exchange of controls, safety pilot, no simulated condition that may jeopardize safe flight). Turns add clearing. The PTS lists failure to clear the area before and while performing maneuvers as a typical reason for an unsatisfactory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]]. See and avoid applies under IFR or VFR when weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]], and the safety pilot needs adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

callout.text: Application: when you fly an overbank for S2, brief a bank and altitude limit, recover well before the airspeed limits, and never fix it by pulling. Disorientation demonstrations should not be flown at low altitude or without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

check.q: Under the hood in a long left turn, your student's altimeter unwinds, the airspeed climbs and she is pulling hard. What do you say first?
check.a: "Diving spiral: shallow the bank." Coordinated aileron and rudder first, hold or slightly relax back pressure, and reduce power if speed builds fast; pulling only tightens the turn [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

**Improper cross-check procedures.**

check.q: The examiner, flying, rolls out and the heading drifts left while the attitude indicator shows wings level and the ball is centered. He says, "Must be turbulence." What do you say?
check.a: That is failure to check for precession: with a level attitude indicator, a changing heading and a centered ball, the attitude gyro has precessed. Center the ball, stop the heading change on the heading indicator, and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

check.q: Your student loses 100 feet on every roll-in and gains 80 on every roll-out. Name both errors and the one idea behind them.
check.a: Failure to change pitch as the vertical lift component changes on entry, and failure to adjust pitch as it increases on the roll-out [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. The idea: bank reduces vertical lift, so pitch goes up on the roll-in and back down on the roll-out [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

chunks.title: Building the turn lesson: from VFR habits to instrument habits

body.p: Instrument turns build on VFR turns, so plan from known to unknown: when a skill relates to procedures already learned, the known-to-unknown strategy is effective, and when several skills are taught together, simple-to-complex works well [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Expect transfer both ways: learning skill A can help or hinder skill B, so know the student's past experience [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Application: a VFR habit of 30° banks fights the standard-rate habit; name it on the ground and give her the number for her airplane.

head: Stage
What you do
rows: Brief
Objectives, standards, the end result and safety procedures; invite questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Application: give the standard-rate bank and lead for her airplane
Demonstrate
Explain the power settings and attitudes as you fly, in the same order as the briefing [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Student tells, you fly
She organizes the steps, and you check her understanding before she is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Student tells and does
Thinking aloud shows whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Full panel, then partial panel
Gyros covered [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], or on glass the AHRS simulated [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]; timed turns practiced full panel first [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Correct errors
Get it right the first few times, since faulty habits are hard to correct [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]; safety permitting, let her go part way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
Check understanding

Have her vary the maneuver or combine it with another; a student who lacks the principles usually cannot [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Application: a half-standard-rate turn partial panel, or a turn with a speed change (Task C)

body.p: Sort the error before you fix it. A slip is an error of action; a mistake is an error of thought [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]. Ask the student why it happened and what she could do differently: some errors only need more practice, others point to a method that should change [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]. Visible reminders also help, such as heading bugs for assigned headings [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

callout.text: Application: a turn to the wrong heading is usually a slip; a consistent altitude loss on every entry is usually a mistake about lift. Practice cures the first. An explanation, perhaps with Figure 4-15, cures the second.

check.q: Your student keeps forgetting the assigned heading halfway through turns. Slip or mistake, and what tool does the AIH suggest?
check.a: A slip, an error of action [[25:84|AIH 3-33]], and the IFH ties this error to rushing [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Use a visible reminder: set the heading bug to the assigned heading [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

body.p: In telling-and-doing, demonstrate the turn while explaining the power settings and attitudes, in the order you briefed; if the demonstration strays from the explanation, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The AIH's own level-turn example fits instrument turns too: the ailerons control the roll rate and the bank, the airplane keeps rolling as long as they are deflected, and a lead of half the bank is a starting rule that depends on the turn rate and roll-out rate [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
A full panel talk-through in primary-and-supporting words, 110 knots true, turning left from 360° to 270°:

bullets: "Standard-rate bank is 15 percent of 110, about 16 and a half degrees. The lead is half of that, about 8, so I roll out at 278 [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]."
"Coordinated left aileron and rudder, rolling in slowly enough to keep my scan going [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]."
"About 16 on the attitude indicator; turn coordinator on the standard-rate mark. From here it is my primary bank instrument [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]."
"As the bank comes in, altimeter and VSI: nose up half a bar. Airspeed is primary for power, so a little throttle for the drag [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]."
"Established: trim off the pressures, ball centered [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]."
"Ninety degrees at 3 per second is 30 seconds, so I can leave the heading indicator for about 20 and work pitch, power and trim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]."
"278: roll out at the same rate, attitude indicator primary for bank, nose down as the bank comes off, power back [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]."
"Wings level on 270: heading indicator primary, check for precession, retrim, straight-and-level scan [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]."

body.p: Partial panel, gyros covered: "Turn coordinator for bank from the start, ball centered. Clock instead of heading: roll in as the second hand passes 12, roll out after 30 seconds at the same rate. Altimeter primary for pitch, airspeed for power. Compass once I am level and steady [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]." For a small change: "Thirty degrees right at half standard rate: 20 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]."

On glass with the AHRS working, swap the words: "Turn rate indicator primary for bank, trend vector on the second tick mark; the first tick mark for half standard rate [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]." In control-and-performance words: "Set the bank and pitch on the attitude indicator and the power, trim, cross-check the turn rate, altitude and airspeed, adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]]."

callout.text: Application: the PTS treats an explanation that needs prompting as a typical reason for an unsatisfactory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]]. Rehearse this script under the hood with a safety pilot until the numbers come without thinking, and practice naming a deviation the moment it happens.

check.q: In your demo, the turn coordinator shows slightly more than standard rate at the bank you briefed. What do you say and do?
check.a: Say so at once, because a demonstration that departs from the explanation should be acknowledged and explained [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Then shallow the bank until the turn coordinator shows standard rate, and note that bank on the attitude indicator [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

scenario.title: Instrument turns for a pilot who learned VFR at 30° of bank
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument student, a private pilot with 140 hours, learned to fly in the club's fixed-pitch trainer, which cruises at about 110 knots true. It has a six-pack panel, one vacuum pump for the attitude and heading indicators and an electric turn coordinator. She turns with 30° of bank by habit. Today's plan is standard-rate and half-standard-rate turns, full panel and then partial panel, in VMC with 8 miles visibility, with her under a view-limiting device and you as safety pilot. Next month she moves to the club's glass-panel airplane.

questions.q: On the ground, what standard-rate bank and lead do you give her, and how do you handle her 30° habit?
questions.a: About 16.5° by the 15 percent rule [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] and a lead of about 8°, half the bank [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Name the old habit on the ground: learning one skill can hinder another, so plan for transfer and know her past experience [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Tell her any rule is only a start; she adjusts the bank until the turn coordinator shows standard rate [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

questions.q: Her first turns overshoot the heading by 10° and each entry costs 100 feet. What do you see, and what do you say?
questions.a: She rolls in too fast and overbanks, which brings heading overshoots and pitch errors [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]], and she does not raise the pitch as vertical lift drops [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Slow the roll to the pace of her cross-check, check pitch as soon as bank pressure starts, and raise the nose about half a bar [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

questions.q: In a left turn the ball sits left of center. She asks whether it matters under the hood. What do you answer?
questions.a: Yes. The ball is toward the turn, so she is slipping, banked too much for the rate of turn; add left rudder or reduce the bank [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]. Slips and skids also give a false sensation of banking or tilting [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

questions.q: You cover the attitude and heading indicators and ask for a turn from 090° to 060° at half standard rate. What should she do?
questions.a: A timed turn: 30° at half standard rate (45° in 30 seconds) takes 20 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Roll in as the second hand passes a cardinal point, hold the turn coordinator at the calibrated half-rate picture with the ball centered, roll out at the same rate when time is up, then read the compass once straight and steady [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

questions.q: After a good partial panel turn she relaxes and drifts 150 feet low. In the debrief she says the whole lesson went badly. How do you handle both?
questions.a: In flight, name it: failure to keep the straight-and-level cross-check after the roll-out, which commonly follows a perfectly executed turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. In the debrief, collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then a discussion comparing it with yours, judging each element against standards for her stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

questions.q: Next month she moves to glass. What will you tell her changes for turns?
questions.a: The turn rate indicator becomes primary for bank and the attitude indicator sets the bank [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]; half standard rate is the trend vector on the first tick mark [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]; and an AHRS failure takes attitude and heading, and in the IFH example the slip/skid indicator, leaving timed turns as the simpler tool [[23:217|IFH 7-56]] [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

skills.do: From the right seat, fly standard-rate and half-standard-rate turns to headings to the instrument pilot skill level while explaining, in your chosen method's words, the bank for the true airspeed, the roll-in, the primary instrument in each phase, the pitch, power and trim changes, the lead and the roll-out; first full panel, then partial panel with timed turns, on the panel you fly.
skills.practice: Rehearse the talk-through in the last chunk aloud under the hood with a qualified safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], in the order you brief it, after calibrating your own turn coordinator or trend vector picture in each direction [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

skills.do: When the evaluator flies a turn error, say what you see on the instruments, name the error from the IFH list, explain its cause and give the fix, then demonstrate the fix if asked.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the IFH analog turn errors [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] and the glass turn errors [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] [[23:213|IFH 7-52]] for each other, with a briefed bank and altitude limit and nothing that could jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

quiz.q: Your student flies her trainer at 120 knots true. Using the IFH 15 percent rule, what bank should she set for a standard-rate turn?
options: Only about 12°
About 18° of bank
About 24° of bank
Her usual VFR bank of 30°
quiz.why: 15 percent of 120: 120 ÷ 10 = 12, plus half of 12 = 18° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. A 30° VFR bank is far too much: Figure 4-15 shows 30° at 100 knots giving 6.5° per second [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

quiz.q: A student asks why she has seen two different standard-rate bank rules, both credited to the IFH. What is accurate?
options: IFH 4-11 uses ÷ 10 + 7; IFH 7-19 uses 15%
Both are one formula, written twice
One is for glass, one for round dials
The ÷ 10 + 7 rule is for ground speed only
quiz.why: IFH 4-11 says divide the airspeed by ten and add 7 [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]; IFH 7-19 says 15 percent of the true airspeed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. The glass chapter repeats the 15 percent rule [[23:212|IFH 7-51]], so it is not a panel split, and the two agree only near 140 knots.

quiz.q: Your student asks which instrument is primary for bank once her standard-rate turn on round dials is established. What do you answer?
options: Attitude indicator
Heading indicator
Turn coordinator
Magnetic compass
quiz.why: Set the approximate bank on the attitude indicator, then hold the rate using the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft as primary and the attitude indicator as supporting [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. The attitude indicator is primary again when the roll-out starts, and the heading indicator only once the wings are about level, even though Figure 7-33 also labels it "Primary bank" [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

quiz.q: With 15° of bank, your glass student is turning right from 030° to 120°. Per the IFH example, where does she start the roll-out?
options: At about 105°
Right at 120°
At about 127°
At about 112°
quiz.why: Lead by half the bank: 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5°, so 120 - 7.5 = 112.5° [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. Waiting for 120° overshoots, because a coordinated bank keeps turning until it is rolled out [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

quiz.q: Partial panel with the gyros covered, your student makes a 45° heading change at half standard rate. When does she roll out?
options: After 15 seconds
When the compass shows the heading
After 30 seconds by the clock
When the ball comes back to center
quiz.why: Half standard rate turns 45° in 30 seconds; the clock replaces the heading indicator, and the roll-out starts when the computed time is up [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. The compass is read only in straight, unaccelerated flight [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

quiz.q: Your glass student wants a half-standard-rate turn. Where on this display should the turn rate trend vector sit?
options: On the first tick mark
On the second tick mark
Past the second tick mark
On the course pointer
quiz.why: Position the trend vector on the first tick mark for half standard rate; the second tick mark is standard rate, and past it the turn is faster than standard [[23:159|IFH 6-26]] [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

quiz.q: In a right standard-rate turn the ball is displaced to the right. What does the IFH say to do?
options: Add left rudder or increase the bank
Add right rudder or reduce the bank
Raise the nose to stop the slip
Trim nose-down and wait
quiz.why: The ball toward the turn shows a slip: add rudder on that side or reduce the bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]. Relaxing rudder or adding bank is the fix for a skid, where the ball is outside the turn [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

quiz.q: Your student loses about 100 feet on every turn entry. Which IFH fault fits best?
options: Pitch changed before it was needed
An overbank into a diving spiral
Precession not checked after roll-out
Pitch not raised as vertical lift drops
quiz.why: Failure to change pitch as the vertical lift component changes gives a consistent altitude loss on entries [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Changing pitch too early is the opposite fault, premature back pressure on entry [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

quiz.q: Your student's panel looks like this and she is pulling back hard. What is the first action you teach?
options: Shallow the bank, coordinated
Pull to raise the nose
Add full power to stop the descent
Level the wings with rudder alone
quiz.why: Altimeter and VSI moving rapidly down with airspeed rising despite back pressure is a diving spiral. Shallow the bank at once with coordinated aileron and rudder, hold or slightly relax elevator pressure, and reduce power if the speed builds fast [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. More back pressure only tightens the turn [[23:184|IFH 7-23]].

quiz.q: Your glass student's AHRS is simulated failed. Why does the IFH prefer timed turns to compass turns here?
options: The compass stops working when the AHRS fails
A regulation requires timed turns
Simpler: no compass errors to allow for
The standby gyro still shows heading
quiz.why: After an AHRS or magnetometer failure the compass still gives heading, but timed turns are used because they are simpler: they need no allowance for compass errors [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. The compass needs no other power source [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

quiz.q: Your student holds standard rate well but stares at the heading indicator through every 90° turn. What do you teach?
options: Keep watching it all the way around
Leave it out of the scan for about 20 seconds
Fly the turn on the compass instead
Use 30° of bank to finish sooner
quiz.why: That is fixation on a single bank instrument: at 3° per second the turn will not reach the lead point for about 20 seconds, so check pitch, power and trim meanwhile [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. IFH 6-13 gives about 25 seconds for the same example [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

quiz.q: Your student asks why the IFH wants turns to headings made at standard rate. What is the main reason?
options: It is the steepest bank allowed in IMC
ATC requires it on every IFR flight
It keeps the load factor at exactly 1 G
It leaves time to cross-check
quiz.why: Standard rate gives a timely heading change while leaving time to cross-check and avoid drastic changes in the aerodynamic forces; the airplane should never be maneuvered faster than the pilot can comfortably cross-check [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. Steeper turns are trained too: any turn faster than standard rate counts as steep [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your student slows from 120 to 90 knots in a turn and keeps the same bank. What happens to her rate of turn?
options: It increases
It falls
It stays the same
It drops to half
final_quiz.why: If speed decreases without changing the bank, the rate of turn increases [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. To keep standard rate while slowing, decrease the bank [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

final_quiz.q: Using the IFH 4-11 rule, airspeed ÷ 10 + 7, what bank gives standard rate at 90 knots?
options: About 9°
About 13.5°
About 16°
About 20°
final_quiz.why: 90 ÷ 10 + 7 = 16°, the IFH's own example [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. 13.5° is the answer of the other IFH rule, 15 percent of TAS [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]; the two rules agree only near 140 knots.

final_quiz.q: The PFD shows 120 knots on the airspeed tape and TAS 126 knots. Which number goes into the 15 percent rule?
options: 120 knots, the indicated airspeed
126 knots, the true airspeed
The ground speed from the GPS
Either, since bank ignores speed
final_quiz.why: The rule is 15 percent of the true airspeed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]], and the PHAK rate-of-turn formula uses TAS [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. Bank for a given rate does depend on speed [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

final_quiz.q: Why does an airplane at 400 mph need about 44° of bank for a standard-rate turn?
options: A rule sets 30° as the minimum for jets
Fast airplanes have more adverse yaw
Its turn coordinator is calibrated in mph
The same bank gives less rate at a higher TAS
final_quiz.why: To keep a given rate of turn the bank must vary with airspeed; at 400 mph a standard-rate turn takes about 44° [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]. If the speed increases at the same bank, the rate of turn decreases [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].

final_quiz.q: Your student needs a 10° heading change. What bank does the rule that IFH 7-52 calls better defined give?
options: About 10°
Standard rate
About 5°
About 20°
final_quiz.why: Half the degrees of heading change, but never more than standard rate [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]. 10° is only the upper limit of the general rule, and 20° for a 10° change normally overshoots [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

final_quiz.q: Your student starts the roll-out of a standard-rate turn on round dials. Which instrument is now primary for bank?
options: The attitude indicator
The turn coordinator
The heading indicator
The magnetic compass
final_quiz.why: Upon initiation of the turn recovery, the attitude indicator becomes the primary bank instrument; once the airplane is about level, the heading indicator is primary [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. The turn coordinator was primary only while the turn was established.

final_quiz.q: On a PFD, why does the IFH make the turn rate indicator primary for bank in a standard-rate turn?
options: The roll scale has no 10° or 20° marks
The attitude display is unreliable in a turn
It is the only instrument showing heading
Only it shows standard rate exactly
final_quiz.why: The turn rate indicator is the only instrument that can specifically indicate a standard-rate turn; the attitude indicator sets the bank as a control instrument and supports [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. The roll scale is marked at 10°, 20° and more [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].

final_quiz.q: Calibrating with the clock, your student finds the airplane turns 36° every 10 seconds with the miniature aircraft on the standard-rate mark. What next?
options: Use a larger deflection
Use a smaller deflection
Nothing; 36° is close enough
Use only compass turns
final_quiz.why: A true standard-rate turn changes 30° in 10 seconds. If it turns more, a smaller deflection is needed; calibrate in each direction and use the corrected deflections in all timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

final_quiz.q: This is your glass student's PFD after a simulated AHRS failure. What has she lost that matters most in a turn?
options: The airspeed and altitude tapes
Attitude, heading and the slip/skid
Only the moving map on the MFD
The vertical speed tape and trend
final_quiz.why: An AHRS failure removes all attitude and heading indications on the PFD, and in the IFH example the slip/skid indicator is gone with no standby turn coordinator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The altimeter and VSI tape still work [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

final_quiz.q: Your student asks what a slipping turn actually is. What do you answer?
options: Turning faster than its bank angle would give
Coordinated, but out of trim
Yawed inward by too much rudder
Banked too much for the rate of turn
final_quiz.why: In a slipping turn the airplane is banked too much for the rate of turn and falls to the inside [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. The PHAK adds that a slipping airplane is yawed toward the outside of the turn [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]. A turn too fast for the bank, with rudder toward the turn to be relaxed, is a skid [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner rolls out of a turn; the heading keeps changing while the attitude indicator shows wings level and the ball is centered. What error is he showing you?
options: Precession not checked
No trim after a power change
An overbanked entry
Too little bank for the change
final_quiz.why: If the heading changes while the attitude indicator shows level flight and the ball is centered, the attitude gyro has precessed; failing to check for it is a listed bank error [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's turn entries are faster than her cross-check, and she ends up tense on the controls. Which trim fault does the IFH describe?
options: Turn trim taken out after the roll-out
Rudder trim set toward the ball
Need for a trim change not recognized
Aileron trim used to hold the bank
final_quiz.why: Failure to recognize the need for a trim change from slow cross-check and interpretation: an entry too rapid for the cross-check leads to confusion and tension [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Taking turn trim out after the turn is correct technique [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your student says she can always feel a turn. What does the IFH say happens in a long constant-rate turn?
options: The turn is felt more strongly with time
The ear senses only the roll-out
Only the eyes can sense any rotation
After 15 to 20 seconds, no turn is felt
final_quiz.why: The fluid in the ear canal takes about 15 to 20 seconds to catch up; in a constant-rate turn the pilot then feels no turn, and the roll-out feels like a turn the other way [[23:71|IFH 3-4]] [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

final_quiz.q: In telling-and-doing, what does the "student tells, instructor does" step give you as the instructor?
options: More time to fly it to standards yourself
A check of her understanding before she flies
A way to skip the demonstration step
A grade to send to the examiner
final_quiz.why: Freed from flying, the learner organizes the steps, and the instructor can evaluate her understanding and correct a misunderstanding before she is absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. It follows the demonstration; it does not replace it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: On a no-gyro radar approach, when will the controller ask for half-standard-rate turns?
options: From the very first vector
Only below 1,000 feet AGL
After the turn onto final
Never; always standard rate
final_quiz.why: Make all turns at standard rate; after the aircraft has been turned onto final approach, the pilot is advised to make turns at half standard rate [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]] [[23:309|IFH 10-18]].

final_quiz.q: Your glass student flies standard rate with her eyes on the turn rate trend vector while her altitude drifts. What does the IFH recommend?
options: A modified radial scan
A rectangular scan only
Watch the altitude tape
Fly by the standby gyro
final_quiz.why: Fixation on the turn rate indicator is a major error; a modified radial scan covers all instruments during the maneuver [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]. Fixation is staring at one instrument, whichever it is, so moving the stare to the altitude tape does not fix it [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

takeaways: Rate of turn comes from bank and true airspeed: the faster the airplane, the more bank for 3° per second.
Standard-rate bank: 15 percent of TAS (IFH 7-19). IFH 4-11 also gives airspeed ÷ 10 + 7; they agree only near 140 knots.
Set the bank on the attitude indicator; the turn coordinator or turn rate indicator has the last word.
Pitch up and power up as the bank comes in, pitch down and power back as it comes out, and trim both ways.
Lead the roll-out by half the bank and roll out at the same rate you rolled in.
Half standard rate: 45° in 30 seconds, or the trend vector on the first tick mark.
Partial panel: turn coordinator and ball for bank, the clock for heading, the compass only in steady flight.
For every error: what you see, its name, its cause, the fix and how you would show it.
cfi_notes: The IFH gives two standard-rate bank rules: 15 percent of TAS, airspeed ÷ 10 plus half [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]], and airspeed ÷ 10 plus 7 [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. They agree near 140 knots; at 90 knots they give 13.5° and 16°. Teach the 15 percent rule, mention the other, and let the turn coordinator or turn rate indicator settle it.

The IFH also gives three small-turn rules: bank about the degrees to turn, not over 30° [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]; no more than the degrees to turn and no more than standard rate [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; and half the change, never more than standard rate [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]. The last is the one the IFH calls better defined.

The fixation example differs slightly: IFH 7-25 says the heading indicator can leave the cross-check for about 20 seconds in a 90° standard-rate turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]], IFH 6-13 says about 25 seconds [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. The teaching point is the same.

Primary bank in an established turn is the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft on round dials [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] and the turn rate indicator on glass, the only instrument that shows standard rate exactly [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. On glass the attitude indicator is primary only when flying a specific bank angle [[23:199|IFH 7-38]]. Examiners like to ask this.

Half standard rate has no IFH bank rule and no mark on an analog turn coordinator; the IFH defines it by time, 45° in 30 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], and on glass by the first tick mark [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]. Have a calibrated picture ready, because the PTS names it in K1b [[FAA-S-8081-9E:32|PTS VI.B K1b]].

IFH 4-11 says trim used in a turn must be removed once the turn is complete [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], and IFH 7-20 says to trim off pressures as the bank is established [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Both agree: trim in, and trim out again.

The IFH glass failure pages show one example airplane, with no standby turn coordinator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]] and a hidden turn coordinator feeding the autopilot [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Other systems differ; teach from the AFM supplement of the airplane you fly.

The PTS lists FAA-H-8083-15 without a suffix [[FAA-S-8081-9E:32|PTS VI.B]]; teach from the current IFH, 8083-15B. The IFH still mentions the instrument PTS [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]; the instrument standard is now the Instrument Rating ACS, FAA-S-ACS-8 [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:3|IR ACS Revision History]], which the CFII PTS itself lists among its references [[FAA-S-8081-9E:8|PTS Introduction]].

Expect the examiner to ask for the bank at a given TAS, the lead, the primary instruments in each phase, a half-standard-rate turn and a partial panel timed turn, and to fly a slip, an altitude loss on entry or an unchecked precession for S2. The PTS also requires a realistic distraction during the flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Use of Distractions During Practical Tests]].
gaps: No source here gives a bank rule of thumb for a half-standard-rate turn or a half-rate mark on an analog turn coordinator; set it with the clock, 45° in 30 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
Pitch attitudes, power settings and the overbanking tendency in turns for a given airplane come from the POH/AFM and practice [[23:162|IFH 7-1]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

The IFH does not say which instrument gives bank for a timed turn after an AHRS failure has also removed the turn rate indicator; in its example only the standby attitude indicator is left [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Check the AFM supplement.

The CFII PTS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task beyond the instrument pilot skill level [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]; the Instrument Rating ACS standard is altitude ±100 feet in level flight, selected headings ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots and bank ±5° during turns [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:16|IR ACS IR.IV.A.S1]] (listed in the Instrument lesson IR.IV.A).
No source here says how to simulate an AHRS failure or cover a turn coordinator in a particular airplane; follow the AFM supplement and school procedures.

activities.title: Bank-angle rules of thumb, the IFH way
activities.intro: Use the IFH rule named in each item. Note that the IFH gives two standard-rate bank rules: 15 percent of TAS (IFH 7-19 and 7-51) and airspeed ÷ 10 + 7 (IFH 4-11). Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: 15 percent rule (IFH 7-19): TAS 90 knots. What bank gives standard rate?
The second IFH rule (IFH 4-11, airspeed ÷ 10 + 7): the same 90 knots. What bank?
items.why: 90 ÷ 10 + 7 = 16°, the IFH's own example [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. The two IFH rules differ by 2.5° here; they agree near 140 knots.

items.q: 15 percent rule: the PFD shows TAS 126 knots. Standard-rate bank, to the nearest degree?
items.why: 12.6 + 6.3 = 18.9, about 19° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Use the TAS box, not the 120 knots on the tape, as in Figure 7-67 [[23:213|IFH 7-52]].

items.q: Lead (IFH 7-20): with 18° of bank, how many degrees before the heading do you start the roll-out?
items.why: Lead by half the bank: 18 ÷ 2 = 9° [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Refine it once the roll-in and roll-out rates are consistent [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

items.q: Small turn (IFH 7-52, the better-defined rule): a 12° heading change. What bank?
items.why: Half the degrees of heading change, never more than standard rate: 12 ÷ 2 = 6° [[23:213|IFH 7-52]].

items.q: Timed turn (IFH 7-53): from 120° to 360° at standard rate. How many seconds?
items.why: 120° ÷ 3° per second = 40 seconds, the IFH example [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

items.q: Half standard rate (IFH 7-21): how many seconds for a 30° heading change?
items.why: Half standard rate turns 45° in 30 seconds, so 30° takes 20 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

activities.title: Which instrument is primary for bank right now?
activities.intro: Tap each moment of the turn, then the instrument the IFH makes primary for bank at that moment.
buckets: Turn coordinator or turn rate indicator

items.t: Round dials: rolling in, setting the approximate bank
Round dials: wings approximately level after the turn
Partial panel timed turn with the gyros covered
Glass: wings level after the roll-out

activities.why: Round dials: the attitude indicator sets the approximate bank, the turn coordinator is primary once established, the attitude indicator is primary when the recovery starts, and the heading indicator once level [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Glass: the turn rate indicator is primary in the turn, the attitude indicator during the transition, the heading indicator once the wings are level [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. Timed turns: the turn coordinator is primary for bank [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

activities.title: A standard-rate turn to a heading, full panel
activities.intro: Put the steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Work out the standard-rate bank for the TAS and the roll-out lead
Roll in with coordinated aileron and rudder at a rate your scan can follow
Set the approximate bank on the attitude indicator, raising pitch and adding power as it comes in
Check the turn coordinator for standard rate and fine-tune the bank
As the bank is established, trim off the pitch and power pressures
At the lead point, roll out at the same rate, lowering the pitch
Wings level: heading indicator primary, reset power and retrim
activities.why: Sequence from IFH 7-19 and 7-20 [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]], with the glass version in IFH 7-51 [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

activities.title: True or false: half standard rate and partial panel
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A half-standard-rate turn changes heading 45° in 30 seconds.
On the IFH glass display, the first tick mark beside the lubber line marks standard rate.
cards.why: False. The first tick mark is half standard rate; the second is standard rate [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

cards.s: Partial panel, a turn coordinator on the standard-rate mark proves the airplane is banked.
cards.why: False. Once the roll stops it shows only direction and rate of turn; unless the ball is centered, do not assume the turn comes from a bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

cards.s: In the IFH glass example, a standby turn coordinator is left for the pilot after an AHRS failure.
cards.why: False. There is no standby turn coordinator; the one behind the MFD feeds only the autopilot's roll mode [[23:217|IFH 7-56]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

cards.s: If roll-in and roll-out rates are the same, the entry and recovery time need not be counted in a timed turn.
On a no-gyro radar approach, all turns are half standard rate from the first vector.
cards.why: False. Standard rate until the turn onto final, then half standard rate [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]].

activities.title: Slip, skid or coordinated?
activities.intro: Tap each picture, then the kind of turn it shows.

items.t: Right turn, ball displaced to the right
Left turn, ball displaced to the right
Banked too much for the rate of turn
Rate of turn too great for the bank
Left turn, ball displaced to the left
Right turn, ball displaced to the left

activities.why: Ball toward the turn: slipping, so add rudder on that side or reduce the bank. Ball away from the turn: skidding, so relax rudder toward the turn or increase the bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]. Definitions [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]; the turn is coordinated when the ball is centered [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

activities.title: Read the diving spiral
activities.intro: Your student is in this picture and pulling back. Drag each label to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Steep bank: shallow it first, with coordinated aileron and rudder
Moving rapidly down despite back pressure
Descent: watch for the upward trend as lift returns
Increasing: the third sign of a diving spiral
Reduce power if the airspeed increase is rapid
Turn rate: the bank reference when the gyros are covered

activities.why: Recognition and recovery from IFH 7-23 [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]: altimeter and VSI moving rapidly down with airspeed rising, shallow the bank first, reduce power if the speed builds fast, and the vertical speed trends upward as lift returns. The turn coordinator is primary for bank in a timed turn [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

activities.title: A turn lesson, one call at a time
activities.intro: Your instrument student flies a 110-knot six-pack trainer with an electric turn coordinator. It is VMC and you are the safety pilot.

steps.s: Briefing: she asks what bank to use for a standard-rate turn.
options: About 16 to 17°, then adjust to the turn coordinator
Always 30°, the same as her VFR turns
Whatever bank keeps the VSI at zero
About 5°, to stay safe under the hood
steps.why: 15 percent of 110 is 16.5° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Set it on the attitude indicator, then adjust for standard rate on the turn coordinator [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

steps.s: First turn: she rolls in so fast that the attitude indicator shows 30° before she reacts.
options: Add back pressure to hold the steeper turn
Slow the roll to the pace of her cross-check
Use rudder alone for turns from now on
Ignore it: entry speed does not matter
steps.why: Pilots commonly roll in much too fast; base control pressures on the rate of cross-check, since maneuvering faster only creates corrections [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Overbanking on entry is a listed error [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

steps.s: In a right turn she is holding right rudder and the ball sits outside the turn.
options: Slip: add more right rudder now
Normal: ignore the ball in turns
Skid: relax the right rudder or add bank
Precession: reset the heading indicator
steps.why: A ball away from the turn shows a skid: relax rudder toward the turn or increase the bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]].

steps.s: You cover the gyros. She must turn 45° left at half standard rate.
options: Roll out when the compass shows the new heading
Hold standard rate for 30 seconds instead
Bank 30° so the turn is over sooner
Half-rate picture on the turn coordinator, 30 seconds by the clock
steps.why: Half standard rate turns 45° in 30 seconds, with the clock in place of the heading indicator and the turn coordinator primary for bank [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. The compass is read only once straight and steady [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

steps.s: She rolls out on time, then sits back and loses 150 feet in straight flight.
options: Normal fatigue: end the lesson now
She dropped the straight-and-level cross-check
Compass error: wait for the card to settle
Trim error: roll in nose-up trim at once
steps.why: Failure to maintain the straight-and-level cross-check after the roll-out commonly follows a perfectly executed turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

activities.title: Name that turn error
activities.intro: Tap what you see, then the error the IFH names for it.

pairs.r: Pitch not raised as vertical lift drops
Pitch not lowered as vertical lift returns

pairs.l: 20° of bank for a 10° heading change, and an overshoot
pairs.r: Wrong bank for the heading change

pairs.l: Eyes on the heading indicator all through a 90° turn
pairs.r: Fixation on a single bank instrument

pairs.l: Heading drifts after the roll-out, wings level, ball centered
Tense on the controls after a fast entry
pairs.r: Need for a trim change not recognized

activities.why: Pitch, bank and trim errors from IFH 7-25 and 7-26 [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].
